summary: IGP Flexible Algorithms create constraint-based paths. This RFC defines a generic metric type and a set of bandwidth-related constraints that can be used in them, helping routing follow link capacity and delay.

plainLanguage.summary: Routing protocols choose a path by adding up the metrics of its links. This RFC lets operators advertise any metric they like per link, add two rules that remove links below a bandwidth limit or above a delay limit, and define a bandwidth metric that routers calculate on their own.

subtitle: New link metrics and pruning rules let IS-IS and OSPF Flex-Algorithm steer traffic by bandwidth and delay.

tldr.problem: Routing protocols pick paths by adding up link metrics, and the usual metric is set from link capacity, which does not stop traffic from landing on slow links when something fails. Operators need paths that avoid low-bandwidth and high-delay links outright.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a Generic Metric sub-TLV so that any administrator-defined metric can be advertised per link, two new Flex-Algorithm constraints that prune links below a minimum bandwidth or above a maximum delay, and a Bandwidth Metric that routers can derive automatically from link bandwidth.
tldr.outcome: IS-IS and OSPF can now carry Flex-Algorithm paths that follow capacity and delay limits, and the limits are set centrally in the algorithm definition. The document updates RFC 9350 and has since been updated by RFC 9917.

today: RFC 9843 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2025. It updates RFC 9350 and has since been updated by RFC 9917. It defines the generic metric mechanism, two new Flex-Algorithm constraints and a bandwidth-based metric type.

sections.title: Why Bandwidth and Delay Constraints
sections.content:
High bandwidth traffic, such as residential Internet traffic and machine-to-machine flows, benefits from using high capacity links. Many operators therefore define a link's metric relative to its capacity, to push traffic towards higher bandwidth links. That is not a guarantee that lower bandwidth links will be avoided, especially in failure scenarios.

Interior Gateway Protocols (IGPs) have traditionally computed paths by minimising the sum of the link metrics along the path from source to destination. The metric is administratively defined, but implementations have defaulted to one that is inversely proportional to link bandwidth, which drove traffic to higher bandwidth links at the cost of manual metric manipulation to get the loading an operator wanted.

Different traffic types need different metrics. Flex-Algorithm, defined in RFC 9350, offers a mechanism for constrained paths by defining a set of parameters consisting of calculation type, metric type and a set of constraints, and it already supports the minimum link delay and administratively assigned traffic engineering metrics. This RFC extends that: it defines a family of generic metrics for administrator-assigned metric types, adds Flex-Algorithm constraints that exclude low bandwidth links and high delay links, and defines a bandwidth-based metric type that routers can derive automatically.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers normally pick the path with the lowest total metric. This RFC lets an operator say that certain traffic must stay on fast links, or must avoid slow ones, by adding rules to the path calculation and by letting routers work out a metric from link speed themselves.

sections.title: The Generic Metric Sub-TLV
sections.content:
IS-IS (RFC 1195) and OSPF (RFC 2328) already advertise a metric for each link in their link state advertisements, and several metric types are supported: the Traffic Engineering Default Metric from RFC 5305 and RFC 3630, and the Unidirectional Link Delay from RFC 8570 and RFC 7471. Rather than enumerate every metric that might be useful, such as jitter, reliability or fiscal cost, this RFC specifies a generic mechanism for advertising metrics.

Each generic metric advertisement is per link and per metric type. It consists of a metric-type field and a value. The metric-type field comes from the 'IGP Metric-Type' registry, where types 0 to 127 are standard types assigned by IANA. This document defines a user-defined space of types 128 to 255, which an operator can assign for local use. Implementations MUST support sending and receiving a Generic Metric sub-TLV in Application-Specific Link Attributes (ASLA) encodings, and in TLV 22 and Extended Link Opaque Link State Advertisements and TE-LSAs.

The IS-IS Generic Metric sub-TLV has a 1-octet Type field with the value 17, a 1-octet Length field set to 4, a 1-octet Metric-Type field, and a 3-octet Value field holding a 24-bit unsigned integer from 0 to 16,777,215 (0xFFFFFF). The OSPF Generic Metric sub-TLV, of types 25, 36 and 34, has a 16-bit Type field, a 16-bit Length field set to 8, a 1-octet Metric-Type field, 3 reserved octets that the sender sets to zero and the receiver ignores, and a 4-octet Value field holding a 32-bit unsigned integer from 0 to 4,294,967,295 (0xFFFFFFFF).

A generic metric may be advertised more than once, but for a given metric type it MUST be advertised only once per link, and once per application per link when carried in ASLA. If several instances arrive for the same link and metric type, the one in the lowest-numbered fragment or LSA MUST be used and the rest ignored. Where a legacy metric type exists, such as the IGP Metric or the Traffic Engineering Default Metric, the legacy mechanism MUST be used and a Generic Metric that advertises it MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Both routing protocols gain a small new field that carries one metric value and names which kind of metric it is. Each kind of metric can appear once per link, and metrics that already have their own field keep using it.

sections.title: The Exclude Minimum Bandwidth and Exclude Maximum Delay Constraints
sections.content:
Large high throughput flows are called 'elephant flows'. Directing one down a low bandwidth link might congest that link and cause other critical traffic on it to drop, so it is useful to constrain the topology to links that can carry a minimum amount of bandwidth.

Where the capacity of a low bandwidth link is constant, administrative groups can already achieve this. The problem arises when a Layer 3 link is really a collection of Layer 2 links, a Link Aggregation Group or Layer 2 bundle, because the link bandwidth then varies with the set of active constituent links. Expressing the requirement as a direct constraint on the topology is simpler, and it gives a single centralised point of control when the minimum required bandwidth changes. This RFC therefore defines an Exclude Minimum Bandwidth constraint: when a Flex-Algorithm Definition (FAD) advertises it, a link is pruned from the Flex-Algorithm topology when the link's advertised maximum link bandwidth is below the minimum bandwidth the FAD advertises.

The RFC also defines an Exclude Maximum Link Delay constraint. Applications such as High-Frequency Trading are sensitive to link delays and may perform poorly in networks prone to delay variability, such as those with transparent Layer 2 link recovery mechanisms or satellite links. The maximum link delay is compared with the Min Unidirectional Link Delay, and the link is excluded when that value is higher than the advertised maximum.

Each constraint has its own sub-TLV inside the FAD. In IS-IS the Exclude Minimum Bandwidth sub-TLV has type 6 and length 4, and carries a 4-octet minimum bandwidth in IEEE floating point format with the units in bytes per second. The Exclude Maximum Delay sub-TLV has type 7 and length 3, and carries a 3-octet maximum link delay in microseconds. The OSPF sub-TLVs use the same type values 6 and 7, with 16-bit Type and Length fields, and the Exclude Maximum Delay sub-TLV has one reserved octet that the sender sets to zero.

Each constraint sub-TLV MUST appear only once in a FAD; if it appears more than once, the whole FAD MUST be ignored by the receiver. A link that does not have the Maximum Link Bandwidth or the Min Unidirectional Link Delay advertised MUST NOT be excluded on the basis of that constraint alone.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rules can now remove a link from the paths a Flex-Algorithm may use. One removes links slower than a stated bandwidth, the other removes links slower than a stated delay. A link that does not publish that figure is kept.

sections.title: The Bandwidth Metric
sections.content:
IGP implementations have long made default metric assignments based on link bandwidth. That has proved useful, but it has suffered from different defaults across implementations and from the rapid growth of link bandwidths. With Flex-Algorithm, the administrator can now define a function that produces a metric for each link and have every node compute that metric from its own bandwidth.

This RFC defines a standard metric type for the purpose, the Bandwidth Metric. It MAY be advertised in the Generic Metric sub-TLV with the metric-type set to Bandwidth Metric, and IS-IS and OSPF advertise this type of metric in their link advertisements. It is a link attribute and MUST follow Section 12 of RFC 9350 for its advertisement and processing during Flex-Algorithm calculation.

A Flex-Algorithm uses this metric type by naming it as the metric-type in a FAD TLV. The same FAD TLV may also ask for the bandwidth metric to be computed automatically from each link's advertised bandwidth. An explicit advertisement of a link's bandwidth metric overrides the automatic computation.

The automatic computation assigns a metric from the total link capacity. It is not intended to update a metric from actual traffic flow, so it does not replace what a Path Computation Element (PCE) does in RFC 4655, which has a dynamic view of the network and provides real-time bandwidth management or a distributed bandwidth management protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A new kind of metric is defined, called the Bandwidth Metric. A router can work it out from the link's capacity, or the operator can set it directly on each link. It is based on capacity only, not on how busy the link is right now.

sections.title: Automatic Metric Calculation: Modes and Methods
sections.content:
Automatic metric calculation is used when a FAD names the Bandwidth Metric and the link does not advertise one itself. Because a link's bandwidth can change, there is a possibility of micro-loops while routers learn about the change. This is no different from the IGP's susceptibility to micro-loops during any metric change, and the micro-loop avoidance procedures of the framework in RFC 5715 can be used.

Where two systems have parallel adjacencies, the bandwidth between them is the sum of the bandwidth of the parallel links, and there are two modes for computing it. In Simple Mode, the Maximum Link Bandwidth of a single Layer 3 link is used, which suits deployments without parallel Layer 3 links. If a Layer 3 link is made up of a Layer 2 bundle, the link bandwidth is the sum of the bandwidths of the working components and may vary with Layer 2 link failures. In Interface Group Mode, a node MUST compute the aggregate bandwidth of all parallel adjacencies, MUST derive the metric from that aggregate, and MUST apply the resulting metric to each of the parallel adjacencies. Every node MUST identify the set of parallel links between a pair of nodes from its IGP link advertisements and MUST take their cumulative bandwidth into account.

Two methods turn a bandwidth into a metric. The reference bandwidth method divides a reference bandwidth chosen by the administrator or the implementation by the advertised Maximum Link Bandwidth. Advertising the reference bandwidth in the FAD lets every node compute the metric for every link, and central control of the reference bandwidth simplifies management when it changes. A granularity value is useful here: the link bandwidth is truncated to that granularity before the metric is derived, so small bandwidth changes do not change the metric. The RFC's example gives a reference bandwidth of 1000G and a granularity of 20G, which produces a derived metric of 10 for link bandwidth in the range 100G to 119G.

The bandwidth thresholds method is a staircase mapping instead of a proportional one. The RFC's example assigns metric 100 to bandwidths from 10G to 30G, metric 50 to bandwidths from 30G to 70G, and metric 10 to bandwidths above 70G. The advertisement carries a set of threshold values and their associated metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can work out the metric from the link's bandwidth in two ways. It can divide a fixed reference speed by the link speed, or it can use a table that maps ranges of speeds to fixed metric values. When several links run in parallel, the router can also add their speeds up first.

sections.title: Using the Metric and Pruning Links
sections.content:
The rules for deriving the Bandwidth Metric apply only when the winning FAD for the Flex-Algorithm names the metric-type as Bandwidth Metric. If the Generic Metric sub-TLV with the Bandwidth metric-type is advertised for the link, it MUST be used. If it is not advertised and the winning FAD does not ask for automatic calculation, the link is treated as if the Bandwidth Metric were not available for it. If it is not advertised and the winning FAD does ask for automatic calculation, the Bandwidth Metric MUST be computed by those procedures, and if the link bandwidth itself is not advertised, the link MUST be pruned from the Flex-Algorithm calculation.

In IS-IS, the link bandwidth is advertised as sub-sub-TLV 9 of the Flex-Algorithm-specific ASLA sub-TLV. It is also possible to advertise the link bandwidth in sub-TLV 9 of TLVs 22, 222, 23, 223 and 141 together with the L-flag set in the Flex-Algorithm-specific ASLA advertisement. Without either of these advertisements, the bandwidth of the link is not available for Flex-Algorithm purposes.

Two rules are added to the Flex-Algorithm calculation of RFC 9350. The first checks whether an Exclude Minimum Bandwidth rule is part of the Flex-Algorithm definition and, if the link has Maximum Link Bandwidth advertised, whether the link bandwidth satisfies that rule. The second does the same for an Exclude Maximum Delay rule and the Min Unidirectional Link Delay. A link that does not satisfy the rule MUST be pruned from the Flex-Algorithm computation.
sections.plainLanguage: The metric a router uses comes from three places, in order: a value set on the link, an automatic calculation from the link's bandwidth, or nothing at all. Links that break the bandwidth or delay rule are removed from the set of paths the algorithm may choose.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The RFC states that this extension brings no new backward compatibility issues. As described in RFC 9350, any node that does not understand the new sub-TLVs in a FAD TLV stops participation in the corresponding Flex-Algorithm. The new extensions can therefore be deployed among the nodes that are upgraded to understand them without affecting the nodes that are not upgraded.

The new metric advertisements work the same way. As per Section 13 of RFC 9350, when links do not advertise the metric type named by the selected FAD, the link is pruned from Flex-Algorithm calculations. The new metric types, and the Flex-Algorithms that use them, can be deployed without affecting an existing deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that does not understand the new rules simply stops taking part in that Flex-Algorithm, so the new rules can be turned on one part of the network at a time.

sections.title: Security and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 9350 are inherited by this document, and it adds no new ones.

For operations, the operational considerations of RFC 9350 generally apply to these extensions as well. This document defines a metric-type range for user-defined metrics, and when those are used in an inter-area or inter-level network, all the domains should assign the same meaning to the particular metric-type. The YANG data models for the Flex-Algorithm extensions are defined in separate documents for OSPF and IS-IS.

Before a router goes into maintenance, traffic needs to be diverted away from it, which is done by setting the overload bit or by setting link metrics on the router to a high value. For a Generic Metric, the link metrics can be set to the maximum usable metric for OSPF and IS-IS, and traffic will be diverted to a shorter available path. If there are no alternate paths, traffic stays on the router, because links are not removed from the Flex-Algorithm calculation when they are set to a maximum metric.
sections.plainLanguage: The security rules come from the Flex-Algorithm document this one extends. For day-to-day running, the operator has to make sure every part of the network gives the same meaning to a user-defined metric, and a router under maintenance is kept in the path by raising its metrics rather than removing it.
